units.title: Threads, interleavings and memory consistency
outcomes: Explain how threads share an address space while processes isolate state, and what that sharing exposes to scheduling.
Enumerate the legal interleavings of a two-thread increment and name the schedules that lose an update.
Define atomicity, visibility and ordering, and state which guarantees a lock supplies beyond mutual exclusion.
units.why: Programming's asyncio queues and TaskGroup assume threads and tasks already exist. This unit goes one level down to the mechanism they rest on: preemptive scheduling of threads over shared memory. It assumes programming/concurrency-profiling-operations concurrency-models-gil as background and does not re-teach async tasks.

next.note: Mutexes turn the critical section identified here into an enforceable invariant.

study.title: Race Conditions and Critical Sections
study.locator: The Shared Counter Problem; Why count++ Is Not One Step; What is a Race Condition; Race Condition vs Data Race

focus: Threads of one process share code, heap, globals and file descriptors; each thread keeps its own registers, stack and program counter. A process boundary isolates memory, a thread boundary does not.

count++ compiles to load, add and store. Any preemption or parallel execution between those steps can discard one thread's update. The compiler may also collapse the whole loop at -O2; the races unit measures that case.

Atomicity means no visible intermediate state. Visibility means a write becomes observable to another thread. Ordering constrains which orders are observable. A mutex supplies all three for its critical section; a bare flag supplies none.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the read, add and write table for two threads incrementing a shared counter from 5. Show one schedule that ends at 6 and state what each thread read. Then state, from the brute-force count, how many of the 20 legal orders of the six steps end at 6 and how many end at 7.
traps: One run's exact total proves nothing. Optimization level, core placement and timing decide what you see; ThreadSanitizer decides whether a race exists.
Threads and processes do not differ only in creation cost. The defining difference is shared against isolated address space and what must be synchronized as a result.
Atomicity, visibility and ordering are three distinct guarantees. Making a flag visible does not make a read-modify-write atomic.

selfTest.q: Two threads each run read, add, write on a counter holding 5. Which final values are possible, and how do the 20 legal orders split?
selfTest.a: 6 or 7. 18 orders end at 6: every order where both threads read 5 before either writes 6. Only the 2 fully serial orders end at 7. Count verified by enumerating all linear extensions of the two read-add-write chains.

selfTest.q: What state do threads share after pthread_create, and what stays private?
selfTest.a: Shared: the address space (code, heap, globals) and file descriptors. Private: registers, stack, program counter and thread-local storage.

selfTest.q: Why does OSTEP Section 27.5 put -pthread on the build line?
selfTest.a: It sets the required defines and links the threads library. The chapter build is gcc -o main main.c -Wall -pthread; without the flag, thread calls fail to link or misbehave.

selfTest.q: A learner says visibility follows from atomicity. What is the counterexample?
selfTest.a: An atomic store can still stay unobserved by another thread without synchronization (cached value, reordered observation). Atomicity forbids tearing; visibility governs propagation. The running-flag loop needs both.

study.title: pthread and futex contracts
study.locator: pthread_mutex_lock page for blocking acquire and ownership; pthread_cond_wait page for atomic release-and-wait and spurious wakeups; futex(2) for FUTEX_WAIT_PRIVATE and FUTEX_WAKE_PRIVATE

focus: A mutex has an owner: the thread that locks must unlock. A semaphore has no owner: any thread may post. Mixing the two disciplines causes lost wakeups and double releases.
pthread_cond_wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, and holds the mutex again on return. A signal is a hint, not a handoff: Mesa semantics plus spurious wakeups force the while loop.

Uncontended pthread mutexes stay in user space: 1000 lock and unlock pairs issue zero futex calls under strace -c on this machine (Linux x86-64, kernel 7.0.0-38-generic, i9-12900K). A blocked lock issues FUTEX_WAIT_PRIVATE and the unlock wakes it with FUTEX_WAKE_PRIVATE.
One condition variable per predicate: producers wait for not-full, consumers for not-empty. A single CV with if lets a stolen signal consume from an empty buffer, exactly Figure 30.9.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write the lost-wakeup demo in C with gcc 15.2 -O2 -pthread: signal with no waiter, then wait, and show the consumer blocks until a second signal and prints ready=2. Convert the wait to while (ready == 0) and show the consumer prints ready=1 with a -fsanitize=thread build reporting no races. State the compiler, flags and sanitizer with the result.
traps: A signal with no waiter is not queued. If the predicate changed before the wait, the signal is gone; only the while loop over shared state is correct.
Holding a lock across a slow call serializes every contender, but moving the check out of the lock reintroduces check-then-act. Keep exactly the state transition inside.

Published cost tables are trends, not measurements. On this machine an uncontended lock plus increment costs about 11 ns per op and a 4-thread contended one about 47 ns; the contention unit shows how those were measured.

selfTest.q: What does pthread_cond_wait do with the mutex, step by step?
selfTest.a: It atomically releases the mutex and sleeps. On wakeup it reacquires the mutex before returning, so the woken thread holds the mutex when wait returns.

selfTest.q: Two consumers share a buffer of one slot with if instead of while. Walk the failure.
selfTest.a: Consumer Tc1 waits on empty. The producer fills the slot and signals Tc1. Before Tc1 runs, Tc2 consumes the item. Tc1 resumes past the if and gets from an empty buffer; the homework program prints error: tried to get an empty buffer.

selfTest.q: When does a pthread mutex enter the kernel?
selfTest.a: Only on contention: to block in FUTEX_WAIT_PRIVATE or to wake a waiter with FUTEX_WAKE_PRIVATE. Uncontended acquire and release are user-space atomics; 1000 pairs showed zero futex calls.

selfTest.q: Why must the locker be the unlocker for a mutex, while any thread may post a semaphore?
selfTest.a: Ownership lets the implementation track the holder for handoff and error checking. A semaphore is a counter with no holder, so release-by-other is the intended use, as in producer-posts while consumer-waits.

study.title: C11 compare-exchange and memory orders
study.locator: Success and failure semantics with the expected-pointer update rule; then read the linked memory_order page for the six orderings and what relaxed permits

study.title: __atomic builtins for the reproduce step
study.locator: __atomic_compare_exchange and __atomic_load: the expected-pointer update and the __ATOMIC_RELAXED constant

focus: CAS compares and swaps as one hardware step (x86 CMPXCHG). Everything else, the loop, the backoff, the ABA guard, is software around it.
C11 atomic_compare_exchange writes the observed value into expected on failure. Ignoring that update turns a retry loop into an infinite loop or a lost update.
Weak compare-exchange may fail spuriously; use it only inside a retry loop. Strong is for one-shot attempts whose failure the caller treats as a definitive answer.
Relaxed orders one location only; it does not order other memory or publish safely. A bare counter needs no more; a flag that publishes data needs release and acquire.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write the 4-thread CAS-loop counter in C with gcc 15.2 -O2 -pthread (relaxed order, weak compare-exchange): 4 times 500000 increments must total exactly 2000000, and a -fsanitize=thread build must report no races. Then replace the loop body with a plain count++ and show TSan reporting the race even when the total prints correctly. State the compiler, flags and sanitizer with the result.
traps: A CAS success is not a lock. Two CAS loops on different locations compose no atomicity; multi-location updates still need one critical section.
Spinning is not free. Under extreme contention the retry storm can cost more than blocking; the contention unit measures the crossover.
A lock-backed compareAndSet helper demonstrates the loop shape only; it adds no lock-freedom. Name which layer actually retries without blocking.

selfTest.q: Why does the CAS loop re-read after failure instead of retrying the same expected value?
selfTest.a: Failure means another thread changed the location, so the saved expected value is stale. C11 writes the observed value into expected, so the next attempt compares against current state.

selfTest.q: When is weak compare-exchange correct, and when must it be strong?
selfTest.a: Weak inside a retry loop, where a spurious failure costs one more iteration. Strong for a one-shot attempt whose failure the caller treats as a definitive answer.

selfTest.q: A relaxed atomic counter is exact under TSan. Does relaxed also publish a message written before the increment?
selfTest.a: No. Relaxed orders that one location only. Publication needs release on the writer and acquire on the reader.

selfTest.q: Where does the ABA problem bite, and why does the counter escape it?
selfTest.a: ABA bites when a location returns to an old value between a thread's read and its CAS, so the swap succeeds on changed history, for example recycled stack nodes. The counter escapes it because addition commutes: only the value matters, not its history.

study.title: Spurious wakeups in the cond contract
study.locator: pthread_cond_wait page: spurious wakeups and why the predicate must be re-checked

focus: A data race is a property of two accesses; a race condition is a property of an outcome. The synchronized-map get-then-put has no data race and still loses updates.

gcc 15.2 -O2 compiles a plain-global increment loop into one addq per thread, so the classic demo prints the exact total of 4000000 on this machine (Linux x86-64, kernel 7.0.0-38-generic, i9-12900K). The race is still there: TSan reports a read and write on global count in the same run.

volatile restores per-iteration accesses, so the demo loses updates again (six runs land between 2000000 and 2316186, never 4000000), but volatile adds no atomicity or ordering. It is a measurement harness, not a fix.
A condition signal with no waiter is lost, and a wait may return spuriously. Both force the same discipline: wait in a while loop over shared state.
units.reproduce: Build the plain-global counter (2 threads times 2000000) with gcc 15.2 -O2 -pthread: record five runs printing 4000000, then rebuild with -fsanitize=thread and keep the data-race report naming global count. Then build the volatile variant and record six runs, none reaching 4000000. State CPU, kernel, compiler, flags, repeat counts and warm caches with every number.
traps: An exact total is not a proof. Optimization level, core placement and timing move the number; only TSan or a forced schedule settles existence.
Removing the data race does not remove the race condition. Locking each map access still loses the get-then-put update; the sequence needs one critical section.
Sleep-timed reproduction is not deterministic. A passing sleep-timed run can miss the schedule; barriers and sleep-string shims force it.

selfTest.q: The plain counter prints 4000000 five times and TSan reports a race. Which result is the finding?
selfTest.a: The TSan report. The total is one schedule plus one optimization; the race exists on every run regardless of the printed number.

selfTest.q: Can a TSan-clean program still have a race condition? Give the example.
selfTest.a: Yes. Individually locked get and put on a shared map compose a lost update with no unsynchronized access. Zero data races do not imply a correct sequence.

selfTest.q: Why is volatile the wrong fix for the racy counter?
selfTest.a: It restores per-iteration memory traffic so updates interleave visibly, but concurrent read-modify-write stays a data race: still undefined behavior and still lost updates, now merely observable.

selfTest.q: A signal sent before any waiter is lost. Which two mechanisms prevent the loss?
selfTest.a: A predicate re-checked in a while loop, so a thread sleeps only while the state says so; and designs where the state change itself is observable, such as sequence counters or close flags, rather than the bare signal.

study.title: Priority Inversion
study.locator: The Classic Scenario; Case Study: Mars Pathfinder (1997); Solutions to Priority Inversion
study.depth: Premium lesson, covered by your subscription. OSTEP has no priority-inversion locator; this lesson is the vocabulary source.

focus: Deadlock needs all four conditions at once. The prevention you can prove is a global lock order: it deletes the wait-for cycle structurally, not statistically.

Draw threads waiting on locks as directed edges; a cycle means deadlock is possible, and no cycle means it is impossible for that state. The two-mutex opposite-order program has a two-node cycle by construction.
Try-and-back-off breaks hold-and-wait but can livelock: the try-wait vector runs retried 1.0 to 2.3M times over three runs. Backoff calms the storm; ordering removes it.

Starvation is unfair scheduling over time with no cycle and no progress for one thread. Priority inversion is a low-priority holder blocking a high-priority waiter, as in the lesson's Mars Pathfinder case. Livelock is active retry with no progress.
units.reproduce: Build the two-mutex opposite-order program with a pthread barrier forcing the overlap (gcc 15.2 -O2 -pthread): show it hangs past a 5 s timeout on this machine (Linux x86-64, kernel 7.0.0-38-generic, i9-12900K). Draw its two-node wait-for cycle. Then impose one global order (always A before B) and show both threads print and exit 0. State compiler, flags, timeout and repeats.
traps: A timeout does not prove deadlock. A hang with spinning CPU suggests livelock; a silent hang with futex-blocked threads (gdb shows __lll_lock_wait) suggests deadlock. Inspect thread state before naming it.
Lock ordering must cover every path, including callbacks and repeated keys. The executor practice fails if equal keys lock twice on a non-reentrant mutex.
POSIX offers protocol attributes such as priority inheritance, but support varies by build. Check your platform before claiming the inversion fix.

selfTest.q: T1 holds A and wants B; T2 holds B and wants A. Draw the graph and name the broken condition for each standard fix.
selfTest.a: Cycle T1 to B to T2 to A to T1, so deadlock is possible. A global order breaks circular wait; try-and-release breaks hold-and-wait; timeouts break no-preemption.

selfTest.q: How do you tell deadlock from livelock from the outside?
selfTest.a: Deadlock: threads blocked (futex waits, gdb __lll_lock_wait), near-zero CPU. Livelock: threads running and retrying, high CPU, no progress. Starvation: others progress while one thread does not.

selfTest.q: Why does acquiring the smaller key first prevent deadlock for any pair order?
selfTest.a: Every thread acquires in the same global order, so each wait edge runs from a lower-numbered held lock toward a higher-numbered wanted lock. Edges strictly ascend in key id, so no cycle can form.

selfTest.q: What goes wrong if execute(1, 1) locks key 1 twice?
selfTest.a: A non-reentrant mutex deadlocks on the second acquire by the same thread. The problem statement requires acquiring a repeated key once.

study.title: Design Thread-Safe Blocking Queue
study.locator: Approach 1: Single Lock with Conditions; Approach 2: Two-Lock Queue; Solution Comparison

focus: Two predicates, two condition variables: not-full for producers, not-empty for consumers. One CV forces broadcast-on-every-op or risks a stolen signal.

Capacity bounds memory and wait: max queued bytes equal capacity times item size, and a newly admitted item waits at most capacity divided by aggregate service rate, plus one service time. State units with every bound.
Close is a state, not a signal: CLOSED rejects puts, preserves admitted items in FIFO order and wakes all waiters. A bare broadcast without the flag re-sleeps or loses items.
Admission control turns overload into explicit rejection: the rate limiter allows at most limit permits per aligned window, with lookup, reset, check and increment as one atomic operation.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write the closable bounded queue in C with gcc 15.2 -O2 -pthread (capacity 4): 2 producers times 5000 items with 2 consumers must drain exactly 10000 over three runs, post-close put must return -1, take on the drained closed queue must return -1, and the -fsanitize=thread build must be clean. State CPU, kernel, compiler, flags and repeats.
traps: notify_one against notify_all is a correctness choice under close: waking one consumer while producers also wait can stall shutdown. Broadcast on close.
Window edges admit bursts: a fixed-window limiter allows limit permits at the end of one window and limit more at the start of the next. Name the factor of 2 before claiming smoothness.
An unbounded queue plus a slow consumer is a memory leak with a polite name. Bound the queue or bound the wait; bound both when the slice demands it.

selfTest.q: Why two condition variables instead of one?
selfTest.a: Producers and consumers wait for different predicates. With one CV a producer signal can wake another producer, which re-sleeps while consumers stay asleep. At close, broadcast wakes everyone and each re-checks its own predicate.

selfTest.q: Capacity 1000, 8-byte items, 2 workers each serving 50000 items/s. Bound the queued memory and the worst wait of an admitted item.
selfTest.a: Memory: 1000 times 8 = 8000 bytes plus bookkeeping. Wait: at most 1000 items ahead drain at 100000/s, about 10 ms, plus one 20 us service time.

selfTest.q: Close arrives with 3 items queued and 1 producer blocked in put. What must happen?
selfTest.a: The blocked put wakes and fails without adding. The 3 items drain in FIFO order. Takes after drain report closed, and later puts fail immediately.

selfTest.q: Why must the window check, reset, limit check and increment be one atomic operation?
selfTest.a: Otherwise two threads in the same window both observe a count below limit and both consume the last permit, admitting limit plus 1.

practice.note: Free. Your C queue is the reference; now satisfy the judge's in-browser contract.

units.title: Cancellation, deadlines and shutdown state machines
outcomes: Separate cancellation (a request), deadlines (a bound) and shutdown (a state machine), and say which primitive serves each.
Implement drain-or-abort shutdown with a timed wait, a close broadcast and a join, with no leaked thread.
Propagate the first error to the joiner without losing admitted work in drain mode.
units.why: Programming's cancellation unit built TaskGroup deadlines and full-jitter retries in Python. This unit implements the lower half: pthread cancellation points, timed waits as deadlines, and the OPEN, CLOSING, CLOSED machine the service slice shuts down with. It assumes that unit as background; no asyncio is reused.

next.note: A shutdown that passes idle must also pass under load and saturation.
RPC deadlines are this unit's timed wait across a network.

study.title: pthread cancellation and deadline waits
study.locator: pthread_cancel page: deferred cancellation and cancellation points; pthread_cond_timedwait page: absolute deadlines and ETIMEDOUT with predicate re-check

study.title: Thread Pool Pattern
study.locator: Core Components; Implementation; When to Use / When Not to Use

focus: Cancellation is a request the target observes at defined points. A deadline is a bound the waiter enforces with a timed wait plus re-check. Shutdown is a state machine all threads observe. One primitive cannot serve all three.
Timed waits take absolute time and return ETIMEDOUT without changing state. Recompute the predicate and the remaining budget after every return; repeated relative sleeps drift.
Drain keeps admitted work and refuses new work; abort discards and reports. Set the CLOSING flag under the mutex first, then broadcast, then join to prove no thread was left behind.
pthread_cancel acts only at cancellation points and skips cleanup without handlers. Prefer a close flag plus broadcast; reserve cancel for threads blocked where no flag is checked.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write the OPEN, CLOSING, CLOSED drain demo in C with gcc 15.2 -O2 -pthread: one worker, 3 admitted items, close-while-working, 200 ms timed waits. Three runs must print done=3 pending=0 state=2 with admit-after-close=0 on this machine (Linux x86-64, kernel 7.0.0-38-generic, i9-12900K), and the -fsanitize=thread build must be clean.
traps: Double close, double join and post-close admission must each be defined, not merely unlikely. Test all three.
Broadcast before setting the flag wakes threads that re-sleep. Set the flag first, then broadcast, with both under the mutex.
A bare sleep is not a deadline. Without the predicate loop, an early wakeup exits shutdown while work remains, and a late one reports a drain that never happened.

selfTest.q: What is the difference between cancelling a thread and shutting down a queue?
selfTest.a: Cancellation asks one thread to stop at its next cancellation point. Shutdown moves shared state through CLOSING to CLOSED so every thread drains or aborts and the joiner observes completion.

selfTest.q: Why does the timed wait use an absolute deadline, and what must follow ETIMEDOUT?
selfTest.a: Absolute time does not drift across repeated waits. After ETIMEDOUT, re-check the predicate and the state: the timeout alone changes nothing.

selfTest.q: Close sets CLOSING and broadcasts. Why must a woken worker re-check instead of exiting?
selfTest.a: Drain mode still owns admitted items; only an empty queue in CLOSING moves to CLOSED. Exiting on wakeup abandons work.

selfTest.q: Where does the first worker error go?
selfTest.a: Into shared state under the mutex or a joined return value, read by the joiner after all threads exit. Printing from the worker is not propagation.

Stress a mutex-protected structure with randomized threads and report throughput, correctness and retry counts.
Compare lock strategies under matched contention with per-op costs, stating pinning, repeats and cache state.
units.why: Passing once is not passing. This unit makes timing failures reproducible on this hybrid CPU: deterministic shims for the schedule you fear, stress for the ones you did not imagine, and pinned measurements that survive review.

Throughput and tail latency get their full treatment there.

study.title: Coarse-grained vs Fine-grained Locking
study.locator: What is Lock Granularity; Trade-offs Comparison; When to Use Each Approach

focus: Deterministic shims (barriers, sleep strings, condition gates) choose the schedule; stress (many threads, many iterations, varied seeds) samples it. Shim to reproduce, stress to discover.
Pin with taskset and name the cores: unpinned runs migrate across this hybrid CPU and smear the numbers. The reference runs pin 4 threads to cores 0-3.

Report per-op cost, not just totals: 8M mutex increments take about 0.086 s solo (about 10.7 ns per op) and about 0.374 s with 4 contenders (about 46.7 ns per op) on this machine (Linux x86-64, kernel 7.0.0-38-generic, i9-12900K, gcc 15.2 -O2 -pthread, 1 warmup plus 5 timed runs, warm caches). Same work, 4.4 times the per-op cost from contention.
Fairness is a separate axis from throughput: OSTEP 28.4 names it, plain spin locks lack it, and try-back-off buys progress at 1.0 to 2.3M retries across our three vector runs.
units.reproduce: Write the mutex-against-atomic counter from a blank file with gcc 15.2 -O2 -pthread: 8M increments in all four configs (1 thread; 4 threads unpinned; 4 threads with taskset -c 0-3; 8 threads with taskset -c 0-7), 1 warmup plus 5 timed runs each, warm caches. Your table must show the same shape as the reference: solo mutex about 0.086 s, solo atomic about 0.030 s, 4-thread mutex about 0.33 to 0.38 s, exact totals every run. State CPU, kernel, compiler, flags, pinning, repeats and cache state.
traps: Averages hide the tail. Report the range across repeats (try-wait ran 0.13, 0.21 and 0.21 s); a single mean claims a precision the runs do not support.
Oversubscription measures the scheduler, not the lock. Keep threads at or below the pinned cores when comparing strategies.
Stress without an oracle proves nothing. Assert exact totals (mutex, CAS) or exact retry accounting (the try-wait Retries line) on every run.

selfTest.q: What is the difference between a schedule shim and a stress test?
selfTest.a: A shim forces one chosen interleaving (barrier, sleep string) to reproduce a known failure deterministically. Stress samples many unknown interleavings to discover new failures, and needs an independent correctness oracle.

selfTest.q: Your 4-thread mutex run is slower unpinned than pinned to cores 0-3. What changed?
selfTest.a: Thread migration across cores and shared caches adds variable coherence and frequency costs. Pinning fixes placement so repeats compare the lock, not the scheduler. This machine has one NUMA node, so no remote-memory effect is claimed.

selfTest.q: Try-wait is correct but shows 1.0 to 2.3M retries. What does that number tell you?
selfTest.a: Each retry is a failed acquisition plus another attempt: livelock-shaped waste that ordering avoids. Correctness passed; efficiency did not.

selfTest.q: Why 1 warmup plus 5 timed runs instead of a single run?
selfTest.a: Warmup faults pages and warms caches and branch predictors. Repeats expose run-to-run spread from scheduling and frequency scaling.

units.title: Event loops, work stealing and structured concurrency
outcomes: Explain the event loop: one thread, nonblocking event sources, select, and handlers that must never block.
Contrast event loops, thread pools and work stealing, and state when each fits.
units.why: Not every concurrent system needs a thread per connection. This unit closes the section with the alternative the later networking and server designs assume: structure work so completion, not preemption, drives progress.

next.note: Framing over partial reads is the event loop's day job.
Loop shutdown needs the same drain discipline.

study.locator: Sections 33.1 to 33.3: the event loop and select; Sections 33.5 to 33.8: blocking calls, async I/O and state management

study.title: Concurrency Models
study.locator: Model 2: The Event Loop; Comparing the Models; Choosing a Model
study.depth: Premium lesson, covered by your subscription. Read the event-loop model against OSTEP 33; skim the actor and channel models as vocabulary only.

study.title: Thread Pool Pattern
study.locator: Core Components; When to Use / When Not to Use

focus: An event loop removes preemption inside handlers, not concurrency from the system: a blocking call stalls every connection, so Sections 33.5 and 33.6 demand nonblocking or async I/O.
State moves from stacks to explicit records (Section 33.7): harder to write, easier to bound. No locks does not mean no state machine.
Thread pools bound threads and queue the rest; work stealing balances queues across workers. All three still need this section's admission, deadline and shutdown contracts.
units.reproduce: Run the single-threaded selector demo with CPython 3.14.4: two sends over a socket pair arrive as stream chunks [b'on', b'et', b'wo'] and the loop joins them to b'onetwo' with no threads. Then state, closed-book, the two OSTEP problems with events (blocking system calls, state management) and the remedy for the first.
traps: Event-driven does not mean faster. It removes lock overhead and per-connection thread stacks but adds state-machine complexity; throughput still depends on handler cost.
Readiness is not admission. select() reports ready file descriptors; the loop must still bound handler time and queue growth, or one ready source starves the rest.
Structured concurrency (tasks with a defined lifetime and a join) is not fire-and-forget threads. A pool whose workers outlive their owner leaks the shutdown this section just built.

selfTest.q: Why can one blocking read stall a thousand connections on an event loop?
selfTest.a: One thread runs all handlers. A handler that blocks keeps the loop from polling, so ready events for every other connection wait.

selfTest.q: What replaces the call stack for tracking progress across events?
selfTest.a: Explicit per-connection state records updated by each handler. OSTEP 33.7 names state management as the hard part of events.

selfTest.q: When does this section prefer a bounded thread pool over an event loop?
selfTest.a: When handlers do CPU work or call blocking APIs that cannot be made async. The pool bounds threads while the queue bounds waiting work.
